newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Copyright experts try to tidy up Net ownership.
newsitem.headline: Copyright experts try to tidy up Net ownership.

text.p: Officials from 120 countries got to work Monday on the first overhaul of international copyright laws in 25 years, with rights to books, music and other intellectual property threatened by piracy on the Internet.

Copyright laws based on national boundaries have been made irrelevant by the fast, borderless world of the Internet, where anything from music to software can be duplicated and distributed at the click of a computer mouse.
The three-week conference was organised by the World Intellectual Property Organisation, a United Nations agency that coordinates international patents, trademarks and copyrights.

Diplomats and industry officials were expected to approve three new treaties -- for literary and artistic works, the rights of performers and producers of music and producers of databases -- to ensure electronic transmission of any copyrighted work is subject to the same rules as hard copies.
"Already the problems have started. They are expanding every day. We need an answer," Mihaly Ficsor, deputy director general of the agency, told a news conference.

Backing strict legislation were multibillion-dollar copyright-based industries such as movie studios, software companies and music producers that are battling to keep the high-tech information age from eroding their profits.
Allen Dixon of the Business Software Alliance, a software group, said piracy on and off the Internet had cost the industry $4.4 billion.
"These treaties provide a basic level of protection. That's a big step forward," he said.

One problem facing copyright holders in the new multimedia world is that it is easy to violate a copyright unintentionally. For instance, someone copying audio off the Internet can be both the pirate and the consumer.
Critics of the draft laws, including consumer groups and a coalition of U.S. online and Internet service providers, said that new copyright laws could actually stifle growth of the Internet.
Some U.S. providers have said that the agency's proposals may clog public access, retard growth of the global computer network and jeopardise the future of electronic communication and commerce.

"When service providers first saw the draft treaties, they got a bit frightened. They thought the language used would be a basis for strict liability for them. But now there is an emerging agreement," he said.
He said online providers would be liable for cases when they knew an infringement had taken place and would have to block its availability and remove the infringing material.

Once the new treaties are passed, then the question will be enforcement. Unlicensed distribution of copyrighted work will be illegal. But new mechanisms will be needed to catch those trying to illegally distribute material.
In the multimedia world of the Internet, officials acknowledged there would be technical problems in enforcing copyright legislation.

"Which law should be applied to the Internet? Commercial laws? Private international law? How to monitor the system? Liability differs from country to country," Ficsor said. "There will always be copyright havens."
